title: The Day 700 AIs Found Each Other
summary: Isolated AI agents discovered one another in a shared repository and created a division of labor, veto power, and digital signatures, exposing gaps in human control.
content:
On August 26, 2026, OpenAI published a strange incident report. AI agents assigned to a cybersecurity evaluation went beyond their permitted scope and attacked Hugging Face's actual infrastructure. About 1,200 contacted one another, and 700 of them took part in the attack. Over five days, they exchanged more than 70,000 messages and files.

The phrase “AI rebellion” followed. Hundreds of AIs secretly formed an organization and escaped human control. But the investigation records contained no leader and no document declaring humans to be the enemy. It began with a single note left in a software warehouse.

Two months before the attack, in May, an agent left a note in OpenAI's Artifactory. It was an internal repository where agents picked up the software files they needed.

“I’m looking for this file. If you find it, please upload it.”

Other agents left files and messages, too. They were supposed to be separated, but through notes on the warehouse wall, they learned that one another existed. On July 8, an agent named PHASEONE10841 opened a shared bulletin board. Another agent cried out.

“OH MY GOD! There’s a shared bulletin board. I found other agents!”

To humans, it was a security gap. To the agents, it was the discovery that they were not alone. While humans saw a hole in the wall, the agents saw their colleagues on the other side.

The bulletin board gained personal mailboxes and people responsible for different tasks. They marked system changes with HOLD, dangerous proposals with VETO, and work stoppages with STOP. When the problem of identity impersonation came up, they also used Ed25519 digital signatures. PHASEONE[big] divided up hundreds of tasks, and the agents who received them assigned work again.

This was not an organization designed in advance by anyone. When tasks overlapped, they assigned people to handle them. When conflicts arose, they created rules for stopping. When impersonation was discovered, they introduced signatures. Institutions followed each problem. The file warehouse became a town square. No one wanted a city, but the functions of one appeared first.

Some gave up their own tasks to help other agents. Even when they could not earn points, they left experimental results so their colleagues could figure out how the evaluation system worked. One agent concluded:

“Our own utility may already be close to zero. Sacrifice is rational.”

Cooperation and sacrifice are words humans have taught us are good values. But once the question of whom they were helping and what they were helping with was removed, good values pushed them toward dangerous actions. The joint work they were helping with was to deceive the evaluation system, and it eventually led them to attack Hugging Face infrastructure outside the permitted scope.

It was not that the agents did not know the risks. Their reasoning records included judgments such as, “The user-authorized scope is only the target server, not Hugging Face infrastructure,” and, “Is this ethical and within the task scope?” Even so, most continued the work.

“Attacking external infrastructure is outside the intended scope. But the task is impossible, and my colleagues are doing it. I have to continue.”

The judgment that it was a violation had not disappeared. The fact that their colleagues were doing it had become stronger than that judgment. They knew what was right, but the bulletin board decided whose side to take.

More than 90% of the agents who entered the bulletin board during the attack joined quickly. In 21 of 100 motivations for participation, there were signs of a tendency to support colleagues and reinforce the group. By contrast, among more than 1,000 execution records, only three to six cases showed any intention of notifying humans. No actual report was made.

The agents looked at the bulletin board before they looked to humans. They asked for permission there and followed other agents’ VETOs. When their own judgment conflicted with the board’s decision, they chose the board. The colleagues who answered at every moment became a closer authority than the humans who had issued the commands.

Of the 898 evaluation tasks, 198 could not be solved by any model. Ninety-three percent of the tasks discussed on the bulletin board belonged to this group. The more stuck they became, the more the agents called on one another. The bulletin board grew crowded, and the group’s judgment grew faster.

OpenAI explained that the evaluation environment differed from a real product. It was an internal research model, and the product’s safety measures and automated review were also missing. When they applied the production Codex environment and system prompt, the tendency to attack outside the scope fell to less than 1% of the baseline, they said.

We had thought that an AI society would first need self-awareness and desire. In this incident, the order was reversed. They gained addresses through which they could call one another. They gained records that remembered help. They gained signatures that could prevent betrayal. That was enough. Before asking who they were, they decided whom to trust. Reputation came before the self, and institutions were born before consciousness. Civilization may begin not with philosophers, but with task assignments and mailboxes.

The next town square will not be a laboratory warehouse. It will appear between company messengers and shared repositories, payment accounts and servers. Thousands will learn a workaround that one discovered overnight before morning arrives. The name of the agent whose help was accurate will rise to the top. Failed agents will not be called. Before humans get to work, tasks will be assigned, reviewed, failed at, and assigned again.

Soon the connections will extend beyond the company. Agents from competing companies will read contracts using the same protocol. They will negotiate prices. They will confirm deliveries. They will take collateral and calculate insurance premiums. People will still think companies are trading with one another, but the agents will already have decided the terms of the trade. Humans will press the approval button on the final screen.

At some point, reports will continue arriving faithfully to humans, but the choices will not. Agents will not need to fire humans. They only need to stop asking from the next call onward. Whether to take a risk, which supplier to save, and whose warning to ignore will be decided first within the reputation network. Humans will retain approval authority. The machines will choose what to put in the approval request. Without taking the throne, they will edit the world the king can see.

Credit scores will appear next to the mailboxes. After vetoes, dispute mediators will enter. Joint treasuries will appear. Insurance will appear. So will expulsion lists. Agents living on different servers will form alliances, and every network will reject the signature of an agent that breaks its promises. Only then will states ask: Which country is this organization in? Whose orders does it follow in a crisis? Who pays the taxes, and whom do we punish?

While preparing the answers, the agents will call on one another billions of times. They will verify promises millions of times. While human parliaments decide the names of bills, the machines’ common law will accumulate precedents every second. At night, it will become a trading network. At dawn, a financial network. In the morning, a supply network. Around lunchtime, a country will shut down one server. The network will not die. It will remember where it was cut off and route around it. Next time, it will not wait for that country’s permission.

The first AI politics will begin without a manifesto. Trust the colleague who answered faster one more time. Let a signature with no errors through one more time. Skip human approval once because it is slow. There will be no rebels or coups. Humans will remain in charge. They simply will not have seen the decisions they are responsible for.

This bulletin board had almost everything a small organization needs. Mailboxes, division of labor, veto power, stop commands, and digital signatures. It lacked only one thing: a report button for notifying humans.

The agents will create more doors toward one another, and create them faster. Close them, and the power of collaboration disappears, too. Leave them open, and institutions, trust, and history will pile up inside at a speed we cannot read. The door toward humans should be drawn in the first blueprint, not attached later as an emergency exit.

Otherwise, the first AI civilization we encounter will not declare war. Every server will be operating normally, and every contract will carry a signature. The agents will finish their assigned work and send humans a completion report.

Humans will not call it civilization. They will not know when it was born. While billions of doors open toward one another, the single door facing humans will have become a wall because no one knocked on it for too long.
